name: Ireland
description: Ireland is a highly attractive destination for expats, particularly those in the tech, pharma, and finance sectors, due to its strong economy and English-speaking environment. While offering a high quality of life and a rich cultural experience, expats should be prepared for a competitive and often expensive housing market, especially in major cities.
longdescription: Ireland continues to be a popular choice for expats and digital nomads, with a notable increase in arrivals, particularly from the US. The country boasts a thriving economy, particularly in technology, pharmaceuticals, and finance, drawing skilled professionals seeking strong job markets and competitive salaries. Expats enjoy a rich cultural experience with vibrant music, literary, and arts scenes in cities like Dublin, Cork, and Galway. The Irish are generally known for their friendliness and strong sense of community, making integration easier for newcomers. Public healthcare is available once ordinarily resident, and many opt for private insurance to reduce waiting times. The country offers a high quality of life with good public services, a stable economy, and beautiful natural landscapes. However, the cost of living, especially housing in Dublin, is significantly high and presents a major challenge for many, with rental shortages and competitive viewings. Transportation is better in major cities but can be limited in rural areas. While English is the primary language, the native Irish language (Gaeilge) is also official and visible on signs, taught in schools, and spoken in Gaeltacht regions, adding to the unique cultural fabric. The climate is often wet and mild, which can be a point of adjustment for some. Overall, Ireland offers a rewarding expat experience, balancing professional opportunities with a unique cultural lifestyle, provided careful planning is made for the cost of living.

visas.name: For highly skilled (Ireland)
visas.description: For highly skilled workers in occupations experiencing critical skills shortages in Ireland.

visas.name: Ireland Student Visa (Stamp 2)
visas.description: Ireland's student visa (Stamp 2) allows non-EEA nationals enrolled in a full-time course on Ireland's Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP) to live and study in Ireland.
benefits: Study at Irish universities and colleges
Part-time work permitted (20hrs/week term time, 40hrs holidays)

visas.name: Ireland Join Family Visa
visas.description: Ireland's join family visa allows non-EEA nationals to join a family member who is an Irish citizen or legal resident, subject to income, accommodation, and relationship requirements.

visas.name: Ireland Immigrant Investor Programme
visas.description: Ireland's Immigrant Investor Programme grants residence to non-EEA nationals who make a qualifying investment of at least �1 million in an approved Irish enterprise fund or business.
benefits: Right to live, work and study in Ireland
Path to Irish citizenship after 5 years

visas.name: Ireland General Employment Permit
visas.description: Ireland's General Employment Permit allows non-EEA nationals to work in Ireland in occupations experiencing labour shortages, requiring a job offer from an Irish employer paying above the salary threshold.
benefits: Live and work legally in Ireland

Citizenship by Descent.desc:
If one of your parents was born on the island of Ireland and was an Irish citizen at the time of your birth, you are automatically an Irish citizen. You can apply directly for an Irish passport.
If a grandparent was born in Ireland, you can become an Irish citizen by registering your birth on the Foreign Births Register.
If your Irish ancestor is a great-grandparent, you can only claim Irish citizenship by descent if your parent registered on the Foreign Births Register before you were born.

Naturalization.desc:
To apply for naturalization as an adult, you generally need to have lived legally in Ireland for 5 years (reckonable residence) out of the previous 9 years. If you were born in Ireland after December 31, 2004, and do not qualify by birth, you can apply after 5 years of residence.
Periods spent on a student visa or waiting for an international protection application decision do not count towards reckonable residence.

Birthright.desc: If you were born in Ireland on or after January 1, 2005, and neither of your parents were Irish or UK citizens, your entitlement to Irish citizenship by birth depends on your parents' residence status. One parent must have lived in Ireland or Northern Ireland for 3 out of the 4 years before your birth, or have the right to live there without restriction on their period of residence.

Spouse and Family.desc:
You can apply for naturalization if you are married to or in a civil partnership with an Irish citizen and have 3 years of reckonable residence on the island of Ireland, along with being married/in a civil partnership for 3 years.
Family visas are also available for spouses or those in long-term unmarried relationships with Irish citizens, requiring evidence of the relationship and financial support from the sponsor.

tax_advice:
- **Corporate Tax:** A 12.5% rate applies to trading profits for most companies, with a 25% rate for passive income (rent, interest, foreign dividends). Large multinationals with global revenues above €750 million are subject to a 15% minimum corporate tax rate under Pillar Two.
- **Personal Income Tax:** For 2026, the standard rate band for a single filer is €44,000, taxed at 20%. Income above this threshold is taxed at 40%. Ireland does not have state or local income tax.
- **Universal Social Charge (USC):** This is an additional tax on employment income, charged in bands. From January 1, 2026, the ceiling for the 2% USC band will increase from €27,382 to €28,700.
- **Pay Related Social Insurance (PRSI):** Employees pay PRSI at 4.20% (rising to 4.35% from October 1, 2026), while employers contribute 11.25% (rising to 11.40% from October 1, 2026). These contributions also cover healthcare.
- **Value Added Tax (VAT):** The standard VAT rate is 23%. Reduced rates of 13.5% and 9% apply to certain goods and services, including a temporary 9% rate for electricity and gas until December 31, 2030, and for the supply and construction of qualifying apartments.
- **Capital Gains Tax:** A 33% rate applies to capital gains for both companies and individuals.
- **Special Assignee Relief Programme (SARP):** Highly skilled professionals assigned to work in Ireland by an overseas employer may qualify for a tax break, exempting 30% of earnings between €100,000 and €1 million from Irish income tax.
local_tips:
- **Cost of Living:** Ireland, especially Dublin, is considered expensive, with monthly costs for a single person in Dublin ranging from €2,000–€2,800 (excluding rent). Housing is the biggest expense, with one-bedroom city center rents in Dublin running €2,000–€2,600/month. Smaller cities like Cork and Galway are 10-15% cheaper for equivalent positions and living expenses.
- **Language:** English is the primary official language and is widely spoken. Irish (Gaeilge) is the national and first official language, taught in schools, and present on road signs, but generally not essential for daily communication outside of specific Gaeltacht (Irish-speaking) regions.
- **Safety:** Ireland is generally a safe country with a low crime rate, ranking as the third safest country in the world for expats in 2023. Petty theft can occur in busy city centers like Dublin.
- **Registration:** Non-EEA nationals aged 16 or over planning to stay in Ireland for more than 90 days must register with Irish immigration and obtain an Irish Residence Permit (IRP) within 90 days of arrival. The registration fee is €300 per person for initial applications and renewals, payable by credit or debit card.
- **Healthcare:** Public healthcare is available for ordinarily resident individuals, but many expats opt for private insurance to reduce waiting times for non-emergency care.
